new_statements.quote: Dalam bahasa Kubu aspek suprasegmental yang bersifat fonetis atau tidak mempunyai potensi mengubah arti kata adalah tekanan, nada, dan panjang. Di samping tidak mengubah arti, aspek itu juga terdengar dalam kondisi tertentu atau timbulnya dapat diramalkan (Pike, 1947:95). Kata /anjiN/ 'anjing' misalnya, dapat diucapkan sebagai [anjiN], [anjiN], atau [anjiN] (suku kata yang beroleh tekanan, bunyi vokalnya diberi bergaris di bawahnya). Berikut ini diberikan beberapa contoh tekanan pada kata dasar. /ambuN/ -> [ambuN], [ambuN], [ambUN] 'keranjang' /rumput/ -> [rUmpUt], [rUmpUt], [rUmpUt] 'rumput' ... Dari contoh-contoh di atas dapat diambil kesimpulan bahwa bunyi vokal panjang ditemukan pada akhir suku kata yang salah satu suku katanya mendapat tekanan (stress).
new_statements.translation: In Kubu the suprasegmental features that are phonetic, i.e. have no potential to change word meaning, are stress, pitch and length. Besides not changing meaning, they are heard under certain conditions or their occurrence is predictable (Pike 1947:95). The word /anjiN/ 'dog', for example, can be pronounced [ánjiN], [ánjíN] or [anjíN] (the vowel of the syllable that receives stress is underlined [italicised in print: first variant = first vowel, second = both vowels, third = second vowel]). Some examples of stress on root words follow: /ambuN/ -> [ámbuN], [ámbúN], [ambúN] 'basket'; /rumput/ -> [rÚmpUt], [rÚmpÚt], [rUmpÚt] 'grass' ... From the examples above it can be concluded that long vowels are found at the end of a syllable in words one of whose syllables receives stress.

new_statements.relation_note: kubu1239 is not in the catalog and has no existing stress statements; this is the first primary-source statement for the language (nothing to agree or conflict with). It differs in kind from the only nearby statement held by the project, Anderbeck 2008's 'stress regularly falls on the ultimate syllable' for Jambi Malay (jamb1236, a different glottocode, Kubu explicitly excluded there).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress (tekanan) in Kubu is explicitly non-phonemic ('fonetis', never meaning-changing), and no fixed position is given: each disyllabic root cited (/anjiN/, /ambuN/, /rumput/, /induq/, /jonton/, /lambot/, /kumpal/) is recorded in three free variants, with stress on the first syllable, on both syllables, or on the final syllable. Vowel length is likewise non-distinctive and co-occurs with stress ([ba:gan] ~ [bagan], [hi:dUp], [bu:lUh]). 'Nada' (glossed here as loudness of the utterance) is said to depend on speaker-hearer distance and emotional state and in turn to influence stress and vowel length. Only open juncture (#) is treated as phonemic (2.2.2). I code this as no fixed word stress per source (non-contrastive, positionally free); the authors themselves warn (sec. 1.2, p. 9) that suprasegmentals were treated only cursorily ('bunyi suprasegmental disinggung ala kadarnya').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; the 'both syllables stressed' variant ([ámbúN], [rÚmpÚt]) is given as one of three free realisations, not as primary+secondary.
new_statements.exceptions: None as exceptions; variation is attributed to loudness/affect and distance to the hearer. Scope caveat p. 9: the team limited phonology to segmentals and touched suprasegmentals only in passing because of their affective (non-linguistic) conditioning, limited time, and difficulty reaching scattered Kubu groups. Book pp. 122-156 (end of syntax, references, appendices incl. the wordlist and pantun texts) could not be read from the truncated capture; a full-text search for stress/accent the scanned of pp. 1-121 for tekanan/stress/aksen finds only sec. 2.2.
new_statements.identity_note: Dunggio et al. 1985 describe the Kubu of settled groups in South Sumatra: Sungai Jernih (Kec. Muara Rupit) and Sungai Kijang (Kec. Rawas Ulu), Kab. Musi Rawas, and Simpang Bayat (Kec. Bayung Lincir), Kab. Musi Banyuasin, with supplementary visits to Lubuk Regis (Kab. Batanghari) and inland Bangko, Jambi (sec. 1.2, 1.6, book pp. 8, 12-13; at least 12 male informants; fieldwork Sept 1981-Mar 1982, Universitas Sriwijaya team, Palembang). This is the Rawas/Lalan (South Sumatran) Kubu, the same population as McDowell & Anderbeck's Sungai Kijang site, not the Bukit Duabelas Orang Rimba of Jambi described by Sager 2008; Glottolog kubu1239 covers both.

tone_statements.citation: Sitanggang, Natal P. 2022. Intonasi ujaran deklaratif dalam bahasa Kubu [Intonation of declarative utterances in the Kubu language]. In: Prosiding Kongres Internasional Masyarakat Linguistik Indonesia (KIMLI 2021, Makassar, 18-20 Agustus 2021), pp. 247-251. Jakarta: Masyarakat Linguistik Indonesia. doi:10.51817/kimli.vi.58
tone_statements.quote: Pada dasarnya, perbedaan kontur itu tidak menandakan perbedaan makna yang signifikan. [...] KESIMPULAN Berdasarkan sejumlah varian yang tergambar dalam kontur nada BK, tidak tampak kecenderungan tertentu yang signifikan baik pada aspek frekuensi maupun intensitas, yang dapat dijadikan sebagai bentuk pembeda makna secara gramatikal dalam tuturan deklaratif. Namun, apabila dikaitkan dengan modus lain, yakni imperatif dan atau interogatif, kemungkinan terbedakannya makna itu secara gramatikal dapat ditemukan.
tone_statements.translation: Basically, those contour differences do not mark any significant difference in meaning. [...] CONCLUSION: Based on the variants pictured in the pitch contours of Kubu (BK), no particular significant tendency appears, either in frequency or in intensity, that could serve as a grammatical meaning-distinguishing device in declarative utterances. However, when related to other moods, i.e. imperative and/or interrogative, such a grammatical meaning distinction may possibly be found.
tone_statements.locator: p. 249 (discussion of Gambar 3) and p. 250, section 'Kesimpulan'
tone_statements.summary: No contrastive use of pitch found: F0/intensity contours in declaratives vary by speaker without distinguishing meaning; no lexical tone posited (consistent with Dunggio et al. 1985: nada non-phonemic).

sources.citation: Anderbeck, Karl Ronald. 2008. Malay Dialects of the Batanghari River Basin (Jambi, Sumatra). SIL e-Books 6. Dallas: SIL International. 173 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 3.2.1 p. 28 (Jambi Malay phoneme system): 'Stress regularly falls on the ultimate syllable.' fn.22: 'This is true in elicitation mode. Tadmor (p.c.) has suggested that JM accent might more correctly be described as utterance final.' This statement is for Jambi Malay (jamb1236) from the author's own 13 JM sites; Kubu is explicitly excluded from 'Jambi Malay' and treated separately in sec. 3.9 (pp. 54-56) only from secondary wordlists (Maryono et al. 1997), covering *h retention and penultimate schwa > o; Appendix E Kubu wordlists carry no stress marks. Nothing on Kubu stress.
